articleSummary: Shenzhen, China – a five-person family contracted scabies, with Shenzhen dermatology hospitals reporting multiple recent cases and labeling the infection highly contagious. Symptoms include nocturnal, intense itching and red papules/vesicles, especially between fingers, on wrists, underarms, abdomen, and groin; head and face are less affected. Many cases initially misdiagnosed as eczema. Diagnosis relies on dermoscopy or skin scraping to detect mites and skin tunnels. Transmission occurs via close contact; mites can survive 2–3 days off the body, necessitating isolation and environmental disinfection. Treatment combines skin-directed antiparasitics (5-10% sulfur ointment, 5% permethrin cream, 25% benzyl benzoate lotion; may include oral antihistamines) with thorough laundering and decontamination of belongings. Items should be washed at high temperature or sun-dried, fabrics sealed for 72 hours if uncleanable. Close contacts must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection and spread, with emphasis on hygiene and avoidance of shared personal items.

articleSummary: Dengue fever is rising in Kerala, led by Palakkad district. In June, 1,862 dengue cases were laboratory-confirmed and 6,181 are under suspicion; 6 deaths are confirmed, with 9 more deaths being investigated as dengue-related. In six months this year, 19 dengue deaths have been reported; 4,330 cases confirmed and 12,794 suspected. A further 17 dengue deaths lie on the suspected list, which would raise the toll if confirmed. Transmission is driven by Aedes mosquitoes breeding in waterlogged pools from intermittent rains; outbreaks flare with rain and ease in dry spells. Dengue symptoms include headache, muscle/bone/joint pain, abdominal pain, vomiting, and eye pain; falling platelets can cause fainting or death. Beyond dengue, chickenpox and hepatitis A are circulating. So far this year, 28 deaths have occurred from these illnesses; in June, eight chickenpox and five hepatitis A deaths. Saturday saw 16 chickenpox and 35 hepatitis A confirmations; June total chickenpox cases were 2,312 with one related death, and 77 new chickenpox cases were recorded on Saturday.

articleHeadline: Người đàn ông nhiễm vi khuẩn 'ăn thịt người'
articleSummary: Melioidosis caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei infected a 60-year-old man in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Presented with septic shock and pneumonia; blood pressure 70–80 mmHg, heart rate >130 bpm. Initial diagnosis: pneumonia with septic shock; vasopressors and high-flow oxygen were used. Labs confirmed Burkholderia pseudomallei, the so-called 'flesh-eating bacteria'. The patient had long-standing diabetes (>10 years), heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and obesity (BMI ~39). Exposure likely through gardening without PPE, as the bacterium resides in moist soil, especially clay and red soil. Treatment involved targeted antibiotics with high efficacy against this pathogen; after three days BP stabilized and respiratory status improved; discharged after one week. Melioidosis can cause pneumonia, bacteremia, septic shock, soft tissue infections and abscesses; long-term oral antibiotics for 3–6 months are recommended, along with management of chronic diseases. Seek care for fever, cough, dyspnea, or multiple abscesses.

articleHeadline: What Is Typhus?
articleSummary: Typhus is an infection transmitted to humans by lice, fleas, and mites, treatable with antibiotics. Three types are described: endemic (murine) typhus in tropical/subtropical regions spread by fleas from rodents (bacteria: Rickettsia typhi); louse (epidemic) typhus globally, more common in Asia, Africa, and Mexico, with U.S. cases linked to flying squirrels (bacteria: Rickettsia prowazekii); and scrub (bush) typhus in rural northern Australia, Southeast Asia, India, Indonesia, Japan, and China, transmitted by chiggers (Orientia tsutsugamushi). Symptoms vary by type; scrub typhus includes headaches, fever, cough, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, chills, body/muscle aches, a bite-site scab, lymph node inflammation, and rash, with possible severe neurological involvement. Murine typhus is usually milder; mortality drops with timely antibiotics. Untreated typhus can cause long-term effects and rare Brill-Zinsser relapse. Diagnosis uses skin biopsy, immunofluorescence, serology, or PCR. Treatments include tetracycline, doxycycline, and azithromycin. Prevention emphasizes avoiding rodents and wild animals.
notes: 本記事はVerywellHealthの一般向け医学情報サイトであり、特定の感染症アウトブレイク、集積事例、または公衆衛生上の異常事象を報告していません。チフスの疾患分類、地理的分布、臨床症状、治療法の教育的な説明であるため、リアルタイム感染症監視対象外です。

articleSummary: On 2026-06-29, Africa CDC, the World Health Organization, and African Union member states launched the Joint Continental Incident Management Support Team (IMS-T) in Kampala’s Makerere University to bolster Africa’s capacity to respond to public health emergencies, with a focus on Bundibugyo ebolavirus disease. The IMS-T provides a shared operational platform offering integrated technical assistance, operational coordination, and regional expertise to Uganda, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and neighboring at‑risk countries, operating under the principle of 'one team, one plan, one budget.' It covers surveillance, laboratories, case management, infection prevention and control, emergency logistics and operations, risk communication, information management, and partner coordination. Ebola is highly infectious and deadly, with a case‑fatality rate around 50%. Transmission occurs from wildlife to humans via contact with blood, secretions, or contaminated surfaces; past outbreaks include West Africa (2014–2016) starting in Guinea and spreading to Sierra Leone and Liberia.

articleSummary: 1,274 confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and 360 deaths as of June 29, 2026, per Reuters citing local authorities. The outbreak, declared mid-May, is the DRC’s 17th Ebola outbreak and the WHO’s fourth-largest, caused by the Bundibugyo variant for which no vaccine or specific treatment exists. The epicenter is Ituri province in the northeast, with over 90% of cases, but infections have spread to North Kivu and South Kivu and crossed into Uganda, which reported 20 confirmed cases and 2 deaths last week. Challenges include untracked contacts, armed conflict, and crowded eastern refugee camps. Early symptoms resemble influenza, followed by bloody diarrhoea, internal bleeding, and organ failure. ECDC and WHO deem the risk of spread outside affected areas as low.

articleSummary: As of June 29, 2026, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ituri Province faces an Ebola outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus that could become Africa’s largest. Contact tracing is only 30% of the needed 80%, allowing ongoing community transmission; since May there are over 1,100 confirmed cases and more than 250 deaths, with true toll likely higher. Conflict-driven displacement leaves about one million refugees, roughly one-third in camps where an infected person may generate ~120 contacts. Health facilities are overwhelmed, with 95% of emergency beds filled. Africa CDC plans to recruit up to 20,000 locally employed staff to bolster tracing, education, and safe burial practices. No approved Bundibugyo Ebola treatment exists. Trials are comparing Remdesivir alone versus with MBP-134 antibody, and an oral prophylaxis, Obeldevir, will be tested mid-July in about 1,200 participants, with interim results potentially expanding use to all contacts if effective.
notes: Bundibugyo Ebola virus (BDBV)による大規模流行。接触追跡率が目標80%に対し30%に留まり、約100万人の難民（キャンプ内では1人の感染者が約120人の接触者を生じる可能性）が存在することで、国際的拡大リスクが高い。Africa CDCは2万人の地域職員を募集予定。治療薬なし。複数の臨床試験が進行中。

articleSummary: Nashik Mahanagar Palika, under the National Pulse Polio Immunization Campaign, vaccinated 158,161 children aged 0–5 years in the city on Sunday, 28 June. articleSummary: Ebola outbreak activity near Bunia, north‑east Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with Red Cross volunteers conducting dignified burials in protective PPE. At about 11:00 in Shari near Bunia, a deceased man is laid to rest as four Red Cross volunteers perform the burial. Families now alert the Red Cross themselves, reflecting distrust and fear surrounding death. Before any burial, a reconnaissance team assesses sites, engages with community members, and, if deemed safe, deploys the burial team to ensure dignified, secure handling. Volunteers come from local communities—teachers, traders, and health workers—facilitating dialogue but not eliminating rumors. Some residents claim burial teams receive large payments, around $2,000. Security tensions persist, illustrated by a Red Cross hearse with two broken windows after being stoned, signaling ongoing risks to responders amid the outbreak.

articleSummary: HFMD outbreaks in 2026 show April–May peaks higher than last year, with June–July continuing to rise. EV71 vaccination options include Sinovac’s Vero-cell vaccine (Yierlaifu) and Kunming Institute’s diploid-cell vaccine (Yiweifu). No 'gold standard'; WHO 2018 guidance treats cell substrates in parallel, and Chinese guidelines do not crown one as superior. Real-world data show safety differences: Yierlaifu adverse reactions ~1.08% across 45,239 children (71,243 doses), all mild; Yiweifu ~25.44% across 60,115 first doses (2.93% local, 15.20% systemic). Allergy risk favors Yierlaifu (sterile system; host protein <0.1 µg; DNA <0.01 ng; impurity removal >99.8%). Efficacy: antibody responses can appear by day 10 for Yierlaifu (~89.2%); Yiweifu ~2 weeks. Head-to-head in 36–71 months: seroconversion 95.5% (Vero) vs 86.0% (diploid), P<0.001. Durability: ~5 years for Yierlaifu; ~2 years for Yiweifu. Both support HFMD prevention; prioritize timely vaccination.

articleSummary: India faces rising monsoon-related infections as humidity and rain boost bacteria, viruses, and mosquito breeding. articleSummary: SARS-CoV-2 and the bat coronavirus RaTG13 differ by a single amino acid in the OrfB9 protein, a change that determines whether the virus triggers or dampens host immunity. In human cells, the OrfB9 variant found in SARS-CoV-2 disables an immune alarm, permitting replication, whereas the RaTG13 version in bat cells activates an immune response that helps destroy the virus. This microscopic difference helps explain why a coronavirus benign in bats can cause severe disease in humans, contributing to spillover risk during the COVID-19 pandemic. The researchers—Nevan Krogan (UCSF Institute for Quantitative Biosciences) and colleagues from Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Institut Pasteur, and Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center— mapped interactions with human and bat lung-cell proteins, highlighting molecular signatures that may predict cross-species transmission. Context notes the early spillover near the Wuhan market with pangolins as a hypothesized intermediate host. Findings published in Cell Host & Microbe.

articleSummary: On 29 June 2026, in Ituri's Bunia region, a doctor warns that reliance on traditional remedies by people suspected or confirmed with Ebola virus disease delays medical care, fuels transmission within families, and leads to severe complications. articleSummary: China CDC advises summer health precautions for primary and secondary students to prevent gastrointestinal infections, drowning and other hazards. Summer raises gastrointestinal infection risk, with diarrhea the second leading infectious-disease death cause among Chinese children under five. Preventive measures include washing hands with running water at least 20 seconds before meals and after outdoor play, avoiding street-vendor cold dishes and chilled raw foods, segregating raw and cooked foods in the fridge, and thoroughly cooking meat and eggs. To combat obesity and myopia, encourage at least 2 hours of outdoor activity daily, limit sugary drinks, and keep meals regular. Enforce the 20-20-20 eye rule; cap non-study screen time and conduct quarterly vision checks for high-risk children. Drowning risk calls for supervision near water, safety seats and helmets; manage heat illness with shade and hydration. Parents, schools, and communities should coordinate safe summer programs.

articleSummary: Kenyan bats harbor alphacoronavirus CcCoV-KY43, binding the human CEACAM6 receptor to enter alveolar lung cells, revealing a new entry route for alphacoronaviruses beyond APN and ACE2. An international team from the Pirbright Institute, Cambridge, and KEMRI-Wellcome tested 40 spike proteins from 2,714 alphacoronavirus sequences; most did not use known receptors. CEACAM6 is expressed in alveolar type I cells; structural analysis shows KY43 binds this receptor with ~271 nM affinity. Serology of 368 Kenyan donors (2020–2021) showed no evidence of human transmission. Use of pseudotyped particles shows lab entry is not equivalent to transmission. This reshapes alphacoronavirus zoonotic risk and offers a sequence-based way to gauge spillover potential.

articleHeadline: Doctors explain why children are more vulnerable to severe malaria; highlight related risks
articleSummary: Malaria poses heightened risk for children in India, with Anti-Malaria Month highlighting vulnerability. In Delhi, pediatrician Dr Ankur Ohri and internist Dr Amit Prakash Singh explain that malaria parasites destroy red blood cells, reducing oxygen transport, and children’s smaller reserves and higher metabolic rate amplify health declines. Immature immune systems mean limited immunity from repeated exposure, unlike some adults who gain partial protection. Children also spend time outside the home, increasing exposure and reliance on caregivers to recognize symptoms and seek urgent care. Delayed diagnosis or self-treatment can rapidly progress to severe disease, including cerebral malaria with seizures, coma, or lasting brain injury, and can involve breathing difficulties, hypoglycemia, dehydration. Early symptoms: fever, fatigue, irritability, vomiting, poor feeding, which overlap with other illnesses, underscoring the need for preventive measures (mosquito control, insecticide-treated nets) and timely treatment to protect children.
